hints: Start inside the muscle fibre - what store releases ions when an impulse arrives at the neuromuscular junction?
Think about which ion acts as the trigger and which regulatory protein on the thin filament it binds to.
Recall what covers the binding sites on actin at rest, and what happens to that blocking protein when the regulatory protein changes shape.
Now focus on the thick filament - what structure on myosin attaches to the newly exposed site on actin?
Consider how the myosin head moves once attached to pull the thin filament, and what name is given to that pulling movement.
Remember the role of ATP in letting go and resetting - what enzyme activity does the myosin head have?
Link the repeated molecular events to the whole sarcomere - what shortens when actin slides past myosin?
walkthrough:
The calcium trigger**
When a muscle is stimulated, calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm. At rest there is very little calcium around the myofibrils, so this sudden rise is the signal to start contraction.

Unblocking actin**
Calcium ions bind to troponin on the thin filament. This makes troponin change shape and pull tropomyosin away from its blocking position. That exposes the binding sites on actin that myosin needs to attach to.

Forming cross-bridges and the power stroke**
The myosin head binds to actin to form a cross-bridge. The head then tilts, pulling the actin filament along in a power stroke. This is what is meant by sliding filaments - actin slides past myosin, the filaments themselves do not shorten.

ATP resets the cycle**
Myosin heads have ATPase activity and hydrolyse ATP. Energy from ATP lets the head detach from actin and then re-cock back to its original upright orientation, ready to bind again further along. The cycle of attach, pull, detach and re-cock repeats many times, so overlapping increases and the sarcomere shortens.

Final answer: Calcium ions released from sarcoplasmic reticulum; bind to troponin causing it to change shape and move tropomyosin; exposing myosin-binding sites on actin; myosin heads bind to form cross-bridges; myosin head tilts to carry out power stroke pulling actin; ATP hydrolysed by myosin ATPase allows head to detach and re-cock; cycle repeated so sarcomere shortens.

hints: Start at the beginning of the cycle - which pituitary hormone restarts development in the ovary after menstruation?
Think about what structure in the ovary grows in response, and what hormone that growing structure then secretes.
Consider what that ovarian hormone does to the uterus lining, and also how it feeds back to the pituitary at low levels.
Recall what happens around day 14 when that ovarian hormone reaches a very high peak - which second pituitary hormone is then stimulated?
Link that surge in pituitary hormone to the key event in the ovary at the midpoint of the cycle.
Think about what the burst follicle becomes after that event, and which hormone this new structure secretes.
Consider how this second ovarian hormone continues the work on the uterus and how it inhibits the pituitary hormones.
Finish the story - what happens if no implantation occurs to the new ovarian structure and its hormone level, and what is the effect on the uterus?
walkthrough:
FSH starts the cycle**
FSH is secreted by the anterior pituitary. It stimulates the growth and development of a follicle in the ovary. One follicle becomes dominant and continues to mature into a Graafian follicle.

Oestrogen repairs and controls**
The developing follicle secretes oestrogen. Oestrogen stimulates repair and growth of the endometrium after menstruation. At this stage it also inhibits further release of FSH by negative feedback, so only one follicle usually matures.

Oestrogen peak triggers LH surge and ovulation**
Oestrogen rises to a large peak around day 14. This high level now has a stimulatory effect and causes the anterior pituitary to secrete a surge of LH. LH stimulates ovulation, the release of the oocyte from the Graafian follicle, and stimulates the remains of the follicle to develop into the corpus luteum.

Progesterone maintains then menstruation**
The corpus luteum secretes progesterone. Progesterone continues the build-up and then maintains the thick endometrium ready for implantation, and inhibits secretion of LH and FSH. If fertilisation does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone concentration falls, the endometrium can no longer be maintained and breaks down, giving menstrual flow.

Final answer: FSH from anterior pituitary stimulates follicle growth; developing follicle secretes oestrogen which repairs endometrium and inhibits FSH; high oestrogen around day 14 stimulates LH release from anterior pituitary; LH triggers ovulation and formation of corpus luteum; corpus luteum secretes progesterone which maintains/builds up endometrium and inhibits LH and FSH; degeneration of corpus luteum causes progesterone fall so endometrium breaks down (menstruation).
